Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
# MILP for the Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $i, j \in \mathcal{I} = \{1,\dots,n\}$: trains
- $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{1,\dots,S\}$: stations; segments $s \in \mathcal{S}^- = \{1,\dots,S-1\}$ (segment $s$ connects stations $s$ and $s+1$)
- $p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}$: candidate speed profiles for train $i$ on segment $s$
- $\mathrm{dir}(i) \in \{\mathrm{up}, \mathrm{down}\}$: travel direction of train $i$ (assumption: each train runs one direction over the corridor)
- $\mathcal{B} = \{b\}$: the blocked segment (single partial blockage), with blocked track = the track normally used by direction $\mathrm{dir}(b^*)$, where $b^*$ is the direction of the blocked track.

## 2. Parameters

**Timetable / infrastructure**
- $A^0_{i,s}, D^0_{i,s}$: scheduled arrival/departure of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\underline{dw}_{i,s}, \overline{dw}_{i,s}$: min/max dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $h$: minimum headway (min) on a track/segment (assumed uniform; can be split into $h^{dep}, h^{arr}, h^{pass}$)
- $M$: big-M, $M = T^{max}$ = planning horizon length (e.g., $1440$)
- $T_0, T_1$: disruption window on segment $b$
- $w_i > 0$: delay weight of train $i$; $\lambda \ge 0$: energy weight; $P_i \ge 0$: cancellation penalty

**Speed profiles**
- $r_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: running time of profile $p$; $e_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: energy consumption (kWh)

**Derived (preprocessed) parameters**
- $\delta_{i,s} \in \{0,1\} = 1$ if train $i$'s passage of segment $b$ can possibly intersect $[T_0,T_1]$ (i.e., $D^0_{i,s} - \Delta \le T_1$ and $A^0_{i,s+1} + \Delta \ge T_0$ for a slack $\Delta$); rerouting is only offered if $\delta_{i,s}=1$.
- $\Gamma_i \in \{\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\}$: the *opposite* track direction available for rerouting on segment $b$.

## 3. Decision Variables

**Continuous**
- $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: arrival time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: departure time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0$: positive parts of arrival/departure delays (auxiliary)

**Binary**
- $x_{i,s,p} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ uses profile $p$ on segment $s$
- $y_{i,s} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ reroutes to the opposite track on segment $s$
- $o^{dep}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ departs segment $s$ (station $s$) before train $j$
- $o^{arr}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ arrives at station $s+1$ before train $j$
- $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ is cancelled

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} w_i \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \left( \alpha_{i,s} + \beta_{i,s} \right) + \lambda \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}^-} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} e_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} P_i\, c_i
$$

**Linearization of positive parts** (valid since $\alpha,\beta \ge 0$ and minimized):

$$
\alpha_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s} - A^0_{i,s}, \qquad \alpha_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$
$$
\beta_{i,s} \ge d_{i,s} - D^0_{i,s}, \qquad \beta_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Timetable–speed-profile coupling

Running time must equal the selected profile's running time:

$$
a_{i,s+1} \;\ge\; d_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} r_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

Exactly one profile per (non-cancelled) train–segment:

$$
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

### 5.2 Dwell times and station consistency

$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \ge \underline{dw}_{i,s} (1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$
$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \le \overline{dw}_{i,s} + M\, c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$

(For pass-through stations set $\underline{dw}_{i,s}=0$.)

### 5.3 Initial conditions

$$
a_{i,1} = A^0_{i,1} \qquad \forall i
$$
(Assumption: trains enter the corridor at their scheduled origin time; a delayed entry could be modeled by $a_{i,1} \ge A^0_{i,1}$.)

### 5.4 Horizon bounds

$$
0 \le a_{i,s}, d_{i,s} \le M \qquad \forall i, s
$$

### 5.5 Headway constraints — same track, same direction

For every ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, on segment $s$ that use the **same** track (i.e., both not rerouted, or both rerouted on segment $b$), enforce departure and arrival separation via ordering variables:

**Departure separation at station $s$:**
$$
d_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
d_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

**Arrival separation at station $s+1$:**
$$
a_{j,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + h - M\left( o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
a_{i,s+1} \ge a_{j,s+1} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

These pairs are imposed **conditionally on track sharing**. To make the "same track" condition explicit, define the track-usage indicator (linear in variables):

- On a normal segment $s \ne b$: train $i$ uses its normal track; two trains share a track iff $\mathrm{dir}(i) = \mathrm{dir}(j)$. Constraints 5.5 are imposed only for such pairs.
- On the blocked segment $b$: train $i$ uses track $\Gamma_i$ iff $y_{i,b}=1$, else its normal track. Two trains share a track iff:
$$
\mathrm{same}(i,j) = \begin{cases}
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] & s \ne b\\[2pt]
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] (1-y_{i,b})(1-y_{j,b}) + [\mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)]\, y_{i,b}\, y_{j,b} & s = b
\end{cases}
$$

To keep the model linear, introduce auxiliary binaries $u_{i,j} \in \{0,1\}$ ("$i$ and $j$ on the same track on segment $b$") with:

$$
u_{i,j} \ge y_{i,b} + y_{j,b} - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$
$$
u_{i,j} \ge (1-y_{i,b}) + (1-y_{j,b}) - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$

Then the headway constraints 5.5 on segment $b$ are activated by $u_{i,j}$, e.g.:

$$
d_{j,b} \ge d_{i,b} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$
$$
d_{i,b} \ge d_{j,b} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$

(and analogously for $o^{arr}_{i,j,b}$). For $s \ne b$, use the fixed pairing by direction (no $u$ needed).

### 5.6 Rerouting logic

Rerouting only on the blocked segment and only for trains whose passage may hit the disruption window:

$$
y_{i,s} = 0 \qquad \forall i,\; s \ne b
$$
$$
y_{i,b} \le \delta_{i,b} \qquad \forall i
$$

**Disruption-window consistency (optional tightening):** if train $i$ is rerouted, its entry to segment $b$ must lie in the window (otherwise rerouting is pointless and it stays on its own track once reopened):

$$
d_{i,b} \le T_1 + M(1 - y_{i,b}), \qquad d_{i,b} \ge T_0 - M(1 - y_{i,b}) \qquad \forall i: \delta_{i,b}=1
$$

(Assumption: single-track operation on the available track is conflict-free as long as headways 5.5 hold; no explicit signal-block subsections are modeled.)

### 5.7 Cancellation semantics

If $c_i = 1$, all timing and resource constraints of train $i$ are relaxed. This is achieved by:
- the $+c_i$ / $+c_j$ terms in the headway big-Ms (5.5),
- $\sum_p x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i$ (5.1),
- dwell constraints (5.2).

Additionally, fix the times so no phantom delays are counted:

$$
a_{i,s} \le A^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i), \qquad d_{i,s} \le D^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i, s
$$

so a cancelled train contributes zero delay (its $\alpha,\beta$ can be 0) and occupies no resources.

### 5.8 Variable domains

$$
a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}, \alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0; \qquad x_{i,s,p},\, y_{i,s},\, o^{dep}_{i,j,s},\, o^{arr}_{i,j,s},\, u_{i,j},\, c_i \in \{0,1\}
$$

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Coupling (TRP–TSMP):** Constraint 5.1 makes the timetable consistent with the chosen speed profile: the running time $d_{i,s} \to a_{i,s+1}$ must equal $\sum_p r_{i,s,p} x_{i,s,p}$, and exactly one profile is selected. Slower profiles (larger $r$) consume less energy $e$, creating the delay–energy tradeoff resolved by the weighted objective.
- **Disruption handling:** The blocked track on segment $b$ is unavailable during $[T_0,T_1]$; affected trains either wait (delay) or reroute via $y_{i,b}$ onto the opposite track. Because opposite-direction trains may then share one track, the auxiliary $u_{i,j}$ activates headway constraints between conflicting directions — this is the key safety mechanism for bidirectional single-track operation.
- **Ordering variables:** $o^{dep}, o^{arr}$ are standard big-M disjunctions enforcing a total, conflict-free order of trains on each track; the $c_i$ terms deactivate them for cancelled trains.
- **Big-M:** $M$ is set to the planning horizon length (e.g., 1440 min); any value $\ge$ the maximum possible time difference works.
- **Objective:** weighted linear delay (via $\alpha,\beta$ positive parts), weighted energy, and cancellation penalties — all linear, so the model is a pure MILP solvable by branch-and-bound/branch-and-cut.

**Assumptions stated:** uniform headway $h$; one blocked segment/track; fixed train directions; entry times fixed at origin; no station-track (platform) assignment conflicts; no rolling-stock/crew circulation constraints; disruption window fixed and known.

The generated model is largely sound, but I identified a few gaps: (1) the running-time coupling is only a lower bound — a train could idle on the segment, so an upper bound is needed to force consistency with the selected profile; (2) trains that do **not** reroute must be prevented from traversing the blocked track during the disruption window; (3) the delay definition should also capture earliness relative to the schedule when trains are held. Let me request a revision.

messages.content:
# Revised TRSMP MILP (Train Rescheduling with Rerouting and Disruption Window)

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $I = \{1,\dots,n\}$: trains, indexed $i$ (ordered by original timetable departure).
- $S = \{1,\dots,m\}$: track segments, indexed $s$; segment $s$ lies between stations $s$ and $s+1$; $b \in S$ is the **disrupted segment**.
- $P_{i,s}$: set of running-time profiles (routes/speed profiles) available to train $i$ on segment $s$. $P_{i,b}$ includes the normal route and alternative routes.
- $K_s$: set of physical tracks on segment $s$; each profile $p \in P_{i,s}$ uses exactly one track $k(p) \in K_s$ and a direction $\delta(p) \in \{+,-\}$.

## 2. Parameters

- $d^0_{i,s}, a^0_{i,s}$: scheduled departure/arrival times of train $i$ at the boundaries of segment $s$.
- $r_{i,s,p}$: running time of train $i$ on segment $s$ under profile $p$.
- $r^{\min}_{i,b}$: minimum running time of train $i$ on segment $b$ over all profiles (used in the blocking disjunction).
- $w_{i,s}$: minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$.
- $h$: minimum headway (same for all segments; can be generalized to $h_{s,k}$).
- $M_t$: big-M for time constraints, $M_t \ge T^{max}$ (planning horizon length).
- $M_c$: big-M for cancellation relaxation, $M_c \ge T^{max}$.
- $T_0, T_1$: start and end of the disruption window on segment $b$ ($T_0 < T_1 \le T^{max}$).
- $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \theta \ge 0$: weights for total delay, arrival delay, rerouting cost, cancellation penalty.
- $\Delta^{\max}$: maximum allowed delay.

**Assumptions:** all times integer; $M_t, M_c \ge \max_i (a^0_{i,m} + \Delta^{\max})$; every profile $p$ has a well-defined track and direction; headway $h$ applies to trains in the same direction on the same track, and to opposite-direction trains on the same single-track segment (see constraint (H2)).

## 3. Variables

- $d_{i,s} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: departure time of train $i$ at the start of segment $s$.
- $a_{i,s} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: arrival time of train $i$ at the end of segment $s$.
- $x_{i,s,p} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses profile $p$ on segment $s$.
- $y_{i,b} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ reroutes on segment $b$ (uses a non-default profile).
- $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ is cancelled.
- $z_i \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ (non-rerouted, non-cancelled) passes segment $b$ **before** $T_0$; 0 if it passes **after** $T_1$.
- $u_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ departs segment $s$ before train $j$ (ordering variable, defined for pairs sharing a track).

## 4. Objective

$$\min \; \alpha \sum_{i \in I} (a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m}) \;+\; \beta \sum_{i \in I} \max(0,\, a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m} - \Delta^{\max}) \;+\; \gamma \sum_{i \in I} y_{i,b} \;+\; \theta \sum_{i \in I} c_i$$

Linearized with auxiliary $\lambda_i \ge 0$:

$$\min \; \alpha \sum_i (a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m}) + \beta \sum_i \lambda_i + \gamma \sum_i y_{i,b} + \theta \sum_i c_i$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Profile selection** — exactly one profile per segment, unless cancelled:
$$\sum_{p \in P_{i,s}} x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

**(C2) Rerouting definition** (on segment $b$; $p^0$ = default profile):
$$y_{i,b} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,b} \setminus \{p^0\}} x_{i,b,p} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C3) Exact running-time coupling (tightened):**
$$a_{i,s+1} = d_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_{i,s}} r_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

(For cancelled trains the equality is relaxed by $M_c$; for non-cancelled trains the arrival **exactly equals** departure plus the selected profile's running time — no idling on the segment.)

**(C4) Dwell time:**
$$d_{i,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + w_{i,s+1} - M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S \setminus \{m\}$$

**(C5) Timetable lower bounds (no early departure/arrival):**
$$d_{i,s} \ge d^0_{i,s} - M_c\, c_i, \qquad a_{i,s} \ge a^0_{i,s} - M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

**(C6) Maximum delay:**
$$a_{i,m} \le a^0_{i,m} + \Delta^{\max} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C7) Linearization of the max in the objective:**
$$\lambda_i \ge a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m} - \Delta^{\max}, \qquad \lambda_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C8) Headway, same track, same direction.** For each segment $s$, track $k$, and each ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, both using profile(s) with track $k$ and same direction (enforce only when both non-cancelled):

Departure headway:
$$d_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - u_{i,j,s}) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$d_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - (1 - u_{i,j,s})) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

Arrival headway:
$$a_{j,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - u_{i,j,s}) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$a_{i,s+1} \ge a_{j,s+1} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - (1 - u_{i,j,s})) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

where $x^{k+}_{i,s} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,s}:\, k(p)=k,\, \delta(p)=+} x_{i,s,p}$ (analogously $x^{k-}$ for direction $-$; constraints are written for each direction).

**(H2) Headway on segment $b$, opposite directions on the same track.** For pairs $(i,j)$ whose chosen profiles on $b$ use the same track $k$ but opposite directions (this includes pairs where **both** reroute onto the same single track), the whole traversal must not overlap:

$$a_{j,b+1} \le d_{i,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - u_{i,j,b}) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$a_{i,b+1} \le d_{j,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - (1 - u_{i,j,b})) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

where $x^{k}_{i,b} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,b}: k(p)=k} x_{i,b,p}$ (any direction). **Explicitly: these arrival-headway constraints on segment $b$ apply to all pairs sharing a track there, including opposite-direction pairs when both reroute.**

**(C9) Disruption-window blocking.** For each train $i$ that does not reroute and is not cancelled, its traversal of segment $b$ must lie entirely before $T_0$ or entirely after $T_1$:

$$a_{i,b+1} \le T_0 + M_t(1 - z_i) + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$
$$d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1 - M_t\, z_i + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

Interpretation: if $y_{i,b}=0$ and $c_i=0$, then either $z_i=1$ forces $a_{i,b+1} \le T_0$ (clears the segment before the window opens), or $z_i=0$ forces $d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1$ (enters only after reopening; $r^{\min}$ guarantees the train cannot be inside the segment during $[T_0,T_1]$). If the train reroutes or is cancelled, both constraints are relaxed by $M_t y_{i,b}$ and $M_c c_i$ respectively.

**(C10) Variable domains:**
$$d_{i,s}, a_{i,s}, \lambda_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}; \quad x_{i,s,p}, y_{i,b}, c_i, z_i, u_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Explanation of Key Elements

- **(C3)** is the tightened coupling: the two-sided equality (lower bound from the original model plus the new upper bound merged into one equality) forces the traversal time to equal exactly the selected profile's running time; idling on a segment is impossible for non-cancelled trains.
- **(C9)** implements the disruption-window disjunction with a single binary $z_i$ per train; it is active only for non-rerouted, non-cancelled trains, so rerouting or cancellation provides the legal escape from the blockage.
- **(C8)/(H2)** use the ordering binaries $u_{i,j,s}$ with the standard 3-term big-M activation so headways are enforced only between trains actually sharing a track (and, on $b$, also across directions when both reroute onto the same track).
- **Big-M values:** $M_t \ge T^{max}$ (horizon), $M_c \ge T^{max}$; both must dominate any feasible time difference plus headway, e.g. $M_t = M_c = T^{max} + h$ is safe. All constraints are linear; integrality only on the declared binaries and integer times.

response.content:
# MILP for the Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $i, j \in \mathcal{I} = \{1,\dots,n\}$: trains
- $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{1,\dots,S\}$: stations; segments $s \in \mathcal{S}^- = \{1,\dots,S-1\}$ (segment $s$ connects stations $s$ and $s+1$)
- $p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}$: candidate speed profiles for train $i$ on segment $s$
- $\mathrm{dir}(i) \in \{\mathrm{up}, \mathrm{down}\}$: travel direction of train $i$ (assumption: each train runs one direction over the corridor)
- $\mathcal{B} = \{b\}$: the blocked segment (single partial blockage), with blocked track = the track normally used by direction $\mathrm{dir}(b^*)$, where $b^*$ is the direction of the blocked track.

## 2. Parameters

**Timetable / infrastructure**
- $A^0_{i,s}, D^0_{i,s}$: scheduled arrival/departure of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\underline{dw}_{i,s}, \overline{dw}_{i,s}$: min/max dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $h$: minimum headway (min) on a track/segment (assumed uniform; can be split into $h^{dep}, h^{arr}, h^{pass}$)
- $M$: big-M, $M = T^{max}$ = planning horizon length (e.g., $1440$)
- $T_0, T_1$: disruption window on segment $b$
- $w_i > 0$: delay weight of train $i$; $\lambda \ge 0$: energy weight; $P_i \ge 0$: cancellation penalty

**Speed profiles**
- $r_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: running time of profile $p$; $e_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: energy consumption (kWh)

**Derived (preprocessed) parameters**
- $\delta_{i,s} \in \{0,1\} = 1$ if train $i$'s passage of segment $b$ can possibly intersect $[T_0,T_1]$ (i.e., $D^0_{i,s} - \Delta \le T_1$ and $A^0_{i,s+1} + \Delta \ge T_0$ for a slack $\Delta$); rerouting is only offered if $\delta_{i,s}=1$.
- $\Gamma_i \in \{\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\}$: the *opposite* track direction available for rerouting on segment $b$.

## 3. Decision Variables

**Continuous**
- $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: arrival time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: departure time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0$: positive parts of arrival/departure delays (auxiliary)

**Binary**
- $x_{i,s,p} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ uses profile $p$ on segment $s$
- $y_{i,s} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ reroutes to the opposite track on segment $s$
- $o^{dep}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ departs segment $s$ (station $s$) before train $j$
- $o^{arr}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ arrives at station $s+1$ before train $j$
- $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ is cancelled

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} w_i \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \left( \alpha_{i,s} + \beta_{i,s} \right) + \lambda \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}^-} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} e_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} P_i\, c_i
$$

**Linearization of positive parts** (valid since $\alpha,\beta \ge 0$ and minimized):

$$
\alpha_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s} - A^0_{i,s}, \qquad \alpha_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$
$$
\beta_{i,s} \ge d_{i,s} - D^0_{i,s}, \qquad \beta_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Timetable–speed-profile coupling

Running time must equal the selected profile's running time:

$$
a_{i,s+1} \;\ge\; d_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} r_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

Exactly one profile per (non-cancelled) train–segment:

$$
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

### 5.2 Dwell times and station consistency

$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \ge \underline{dw}_{i,s} (1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$
$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \le \overline{dw}_{i,s} + M\, c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$

(For pass-through stations set $\underline{dw}_{i,s}=0$.)

### 5.3 Initial conditions

$$
a_{i,1} = A^0_{i,1} \qquad \forall i
$$
(Assumption: trains enter the corridor at their scheduled origin time; a delayed entry could be modeled by $a_{i,1} \ge A^0_{i,1}$.)

### 5.4 Horizon bounds

$$
0 \le a_{i,s}, d_{i,s} \le M \qquad \forall i, s
$$

### 5.5 Headway constraints — same track, same direction

For every ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, on segment $s$ that use the **same** track (i.e., both not rerouted, or both rerouted on segment $b$), enforce departure and arrival separation via ordering variables:

**Departure separation at station $s$:**
$$
d_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
d_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

**Arrival separation at station $s+1$:**
$$
a_{j,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + h - M\left( o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
a_{i,s+1} \ge a_{j,s+1} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

These pairs are imposed **conditionally on track sharing**. To make the "same track" condition explicit, define the track-usage indicator (linear in variables):

- On a normal segment $s \ne b$: train $i$ uses its normal track; two trains share a track iff $\mathrm{dir}(i) = \mathrm{dir}(j)$. Constraints 5.5 are imposed only for such pairs.
- On the blocked segment $b$: train $i$ uses track $\Gamma_i$ iff $y_{i,b}=1$, else its normal track. Two trains share a track iff:
$$
\mathrm{same}(i,j) = \begin{cases}
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] & s \ne b\\[2pt]
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] (1-y_{i,b})(1-y_{j,b}) + [\mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)]\, y_{i,b}\, y_{j,b} & s = b
\end{cases}
$$

To keep the model linear, introduce auxiliary binaries $u_{i,j} \in \{0,1\}$ ("$i$ and $j$ on the same track on segment $b$") with:

$$
u_{i,j} \ge y_{i,b} + y_{j,b} - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$
$$
u_{i,j} \ge (1-y_{i,b}) + (1-y_{j,b}) - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$

Then the headway constraints 5.5 on segment $b$ are activated by $u_{i,j}$, e.g.:

$$
d_{j,b} \ge d_{i,b} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$
$$
d_{i,b} \ge d_{j,b} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$

(and analogously for $o^{arr}_{i,j,b}$). For $s \ne b$, use the fixed pairing by direction (no $u$ needed).

### 5.6 Rerouting logic

Rerouting only on the blocked segment and only for trains whose passage may hit the disruption window:

$$
y_{i,s} = 0 \qquad \forall i,\; s \ne b
$$
$$
y_{i,b} \le \delta_{i,b} \qquad \forall i
$$

**Disruption-window consistency (optional tightening):** if train $i$ is rerouted, its entry to segment $b$ must lie in the window (otherwise rerouting is pointless and it stays on its own track once reopened):

$$
d_{i,b} \le T_1 + M(1 - y_{i,b}), \qquad d_{i,b} \ge T_0 - M(1 - y_{i,b}) \qquad \forall i: \delta_{i,b}=1
$$

(Assumption: single-track operation on the available track is conflict-free as long as headways 5.5 hold; no explicit signal-block subsections are modeled.)

### 5.7 Cancellation semantics

If $c_i = 1$, all timing and resource constraints of train $i$ are relaxed. This is achieved by:
- the $+c_i$ / $+c_j$ terms in the headway big-Ms (5.5),
- $\sum_p x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i$ (5.1),
- dwell constraints (5.2).

Additionally, fix the times so no phantom delays are counted:

$$
a_{i,s} \le A^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i), \qquad d_{i,s} \le D^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i, s
$$

so a cancelled train contributes zero delay (its $\alpha,\beta$ can be 0) and occupies no resources.

### 5.8 Variable domains

$$
a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}, \alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0; \qquad x_{i,s,p},\, y_{i,s},\, o^{dep}_{i,j,s},\, o^{arr}_{i,j,s},\, u_{i,j},\, c_i \in \{0,1\}
$$

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Coupling (TRP–TSMP):** Constraint 5.1 makes the timetable consistent with the chosen speed profile: the running time $d_{i,s} \to a_{i,s+1}$ must equal $\sum_p r_{i,s,p} x_{i,s,p}$, and exactly one profile is selected. Slower profiles (larger $r$) consume less energy $e$, creating the delay–energy tradeoff resolved by the weighted objective.
- **Disruption handling:** The blocked track on segment $b$ is unavailable during $[T_0,T_1]$; affected trains either wait (delay) or reroute via $y_{i,b}$ onto the opposite track. Because opposite-direction trains may then share one track, the auxiliary $u_{i,j}$ activates headway constraints between conflicting directions — this is the key safety mechanism for bidirectional single-track operation.
- **Ordering variables:** $o^{dep}, o^{arr}$ are standard big-M disjunctions enforcing a total, conflict-free order of trains on each track; the $c_i$ terms deactivate them for cancelled trains.
- **Big-M:** $M$ is set to the planning horizon length (e.g., 1440 min); any value $\ge$ the maximum possible time difference works.
- **Objective:** weighted linear delay (via $\alpha,\beta$ positive parts), weighted energy, and cancellation penalties — all linear, so the model is a pure MILP solvable by branch-and-bound/branch-and-cut.

**Assumptions stated:** uniform headway $h$; one blocked segment/track; fixed train directions; entry times fixed at origin; no station-track (platform) assignment conflicts; no rolling-stock/crew circulation constraints; disruption window fixed and known.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
# MILP for the Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $i, j \in \mathcal{I} = \{1,\dots,n\}$: trains
- $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{1,\dots,S\}$: stations; segments $s \in \mathcal{S}^- = \{1,\dots,S-1\}$ (segment $s$ connects stations $s$ and $s+1$)
- $p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}$: candidate speed profiles for train $i$ on segment $s$
- $\mathrm{dir}(i) \in \{\mathrm{up}, \mathrm{down}\}$: travel direction of train $i$ (assumption: each train runs one direction over the corridor)
- $\mathcal{B} = \{b\}$: the blocked segment (single partial blockage), with blocked track = the track normally used by direction $\mathrm{dir}(b^*)$, where $b^*$ is the direction of the blocked track.

## 2. Parameters

**Timetable / infrastructure**
- $A^0_{i,s}, D^0_{i,s}$: scheduled arrival/departure of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\underline{dw}_{i,s}, \overline{dw}_{i,s}$: min/max dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $h$: minimum headway (min) on a track/segment (assumed uniform; can be split into $h^{dep}, h^{arr}, h^{pass}$)
- $M$: big-M, $M = T^{max}$ = planning horizon length (e.g., $1440$)
- $T_0, T_1$: disruption window on segment $b$
- $w_i > 0$: delay weight of train $i$; $\lambda \ge 0$: energy weight; $P_i \ge 0$: cancellation penalty

**Speed profiles**
- $r_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: running time of profile $p$; $e_{i,s,p} \ge 0$: energy consumption (kWh)

**Derived (preprocessed) parameters**
- $\delta_{i,s} \in \{0,1\} = 1$ if train $i$'s passage of segment $b$ can possibly intersect $[T_0,T_1]$ (i.e., $D^0_{i,s} - \Delta \le T_1$ and $A^0_{i,s+1} + \Delta \ge T_0$ for a slack $\Delta$); rerouting is only offered if $\delta_{i,s}=1$.
- $\Gamma_i \in \{\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\}$: the *opposite* track direction available for rerouting on segment $b$.

## 3. Decision Variables

**Continuous**
- $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: arrival time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: departure time of train $i$ at station $s$
- $\alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0$: positive parts of arrival/departure delays (auxiliary)

**Binary**
- $x_{i,s,p} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ uses profile $p$ on segment $s$
- $y_{i,s} \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ reroutes to the opposite track on segment $s$
- $o^{dep}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ departs segment $s$ (station $s$) before train $j$
- $o^{arr}_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: $=1$ if train $i$ arrives at station $s+1$ before train $j$
- $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: train $i$ is cancelled

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} w_i \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \left( \alpha_{i,s} + \beta_{i,s} \right) + \lambda \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}^-} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} e_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} P_i\, c_i
$$

**Linearization of positive parts** (valid since $\alpha,\beta \ge 0$ and minimized):

$$
\alpha_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s} - A^0_{i,s}, \qquad \alpha_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$
$$
\beta_{i,s} \ge d_{i,s} - D^0_{i,s}, \qquad \beta_{i,s} \ge 0 \quad \forall i, s
$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Timetable–speed-profile coupling

Running time must equal the selected profile's running time:

$$
a_{i,s+1} \;\ge\; d_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} r_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

Exactly one profile per (non-cancelled) train–segment:

$$
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{i,s}} x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}^-
$$

### 5.2 Dwell times and station consistency

$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \ge \underline{dw}_{i,s} (1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$
$$
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s} \le \overline{dw}_{i,s} + M\, c_i \qquad \forall i,\; s \in \mathcal{S}
$$

(For pass-through stations set $\underline{dw}_{i,s}=0$.)

### 5.3 Initial conditions

$$
a_{i,1} = A^0_{i,1} \qquad \forall i
$$
(Assumption: trains enter the corridor at their scheduled origin time; a delayed entry could be modeled by $a_{i,1} \ge A^0_{i,1}$.)

### 5.4 Horizon bounds

$$
0 \le a_{i,s}, d_{i,s} \le M \qquad \forall i, s
$$

### 5.5 Headway constraints — same track, same direction

For every ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, on segment $s$ that use the **same** track (i.e., both not rerouted, or both rerouted on segment $b$), enforce departure and arrival separation via ordering variables:

**Departure separation at station $s$:**
$$
d_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
d_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

**Arrival separation at station $s+1$:**
$$
a_{j,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + h - M\left( o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$
$$
a_{i,s+1} \ge a_{j,s+1} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{arr}_{i,j,s} + c_i + c_j \right) \qquad \forall i<j,\; s
$$

These pairs are imposed **conditionally on track sharing**. To make the "same track" condition explicit, define the track-usage indicator (linear in variables):

- On a normal segment $s \ne b$: train $i$ uses its normal track; two trains share a track iff $\mathrm{dir}(i) = \mathrm{dir}(j)$. Constraints 5.5 are imposed only for such pairs.
- On the blocked segment $b$: train $i$ uses track $\Gamma_i$ iff $y_{i,b}=1$, else its normal track. Two trains share a track iff:
$$
\mathrm{same}(i,j) = \begin{cases}
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] & s \ne b\\[2pt]
[\mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)] (1-y_{i,b})(1-y_{j,b}) + [\mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)]\, y_{i,b}\, y_{j,b} & s = b
\end{cases}
$$

To keep the model linear, introduce auxiliary binaries $u_{i,j} \in \{0,1\}$ ("$i$ and $j$ on the same track on segment $b$") with:

$$
u_{i,j} \ge y_{i,b} + y_{j,b} - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)\ne\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$
$$
u_{i,j} \ge (1-y_{i,b}) + (1-y_{j,b}) - 1, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{i,b}, \quad u_{i,j} \le 1-y_{j,b} \qquad \forall i<j,\; \mathrm{dir}(i)=\mathrm{dir}(j)
$$

Then the headway constraints 5.5 on segment $b$ are activated by $u_{i,j}$, e.g.:

$$
d_{j,b} \ge d_{i,b} + h - M\left( o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$
$$
d_{i,b} \ge d_{j,b} + h - M\left( 1 - o^{dep}_{i,j,b} + (1-u_{i,j}) + c_i + c_j \right)
$$

(and analogously for $o^{arr}_{i,j,b}$). For $s \ne b$, use the fixed pairing by direction (no $u$ needed).

### 5.6 Rerouting logic

Rerouting only on the blocked segment and only for trains whose passage may hit the disruption window:

$$
y_{i,s} = 0 \qquad \forall i,\; s \ne b
$$
$$
y_{i,b} \le \delta_{i,b} \qquad \forall i
$$

**Disruption-window consistency (optional tightening):** if train $i$ is rerouted, its entry to segment $b$ must lie in the window (otherwise rerouting is pointless and it stays on its own track once reopened):

$$
d_{i,b} \le T_1 + M(1 - y_{i,b}), \qquad d_{i,b} \ge T_0 - M(1 - y_{i,b}) \qquad \forall i: \delta_{i,b}=1
$$

(Assumption: single-track operation on the available track is conflict-free as long as headways 5.5 hold; no explicit signal-block subsections are modeled.)

### 5.7 Cancellation semantics

If $c_i = 1$, all timing and resource constraints of train $i$ are relaxed. This is achieved by:
- the $+c_i$ / $+c_j$ terms in the headway big-Ms (5.5),
- $\sum_p x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i$ (5.1),
- dwell constraints (5.2).

Additionally, fix the times so no phantom delays are counted:

$$
a_{i,s} \le A^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i), \qquad d_{i,s} \le D^0_{i,s} + M(1 - c_i) \qquad \forall i, s
$$

so a cancelled train contributes zero delay (its $\alpha,\beta$ can be 0) and occupies no resources.

### 5.8 Variable domains

$$
a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}, \alpha_{i,s}, \beta_{i,s} \ge 0; \qquad x_{i,s,p},\, y_{i,s},\, o^{dep}_{i,j,s},\, o^{arr}_{i,j,s},\, u_{i,j},\, c_i \in \{0,1\}
$$

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

- **Coupling (TRP–TSMP):** Constraint 5.1 makes the timetable consistent with the chosen speed profile: the running time $d_{i,s} \to a_{i,s+1}$ must equal $\sum_p r_{i,s,p} x_{i,s,p}$, and exactly one profile is selected. Slower profiles (larger $r$) consume less energy $e$, creating the delay–energy tradeoff resolved by the weighted objective.
- **Disruption handling:** The blocked track on segment $b$ is unavailable during $[T_0,T_1]$; affected trains either wait (delay) or reroute via $y_{i,b}$ onto the opposite track. Because opposite-direction trains may then share one track, the auxiliary $u_{i,j}$ activates headway constraints between conflicting directions — this is the key safety mechanism for bidirectional single-track operation.
- **Ordering variables:** $o^{dep}, o^{arr}$ are standard big-M disjunctions enforcing a total, conflict-free order of trains on each track; the $c_i$ terms deactivate them for cancelled trains.
- **Big-M:** $M$ is set to the planning horizon length (e.g., 1440 min); any value $\ge$ the maximum possible time difference works.
- **Objective:** weighted linear delay (via $\alpha,\beta$ positive parts), weighted energy, and cancellation penalties — all linear, so the model is a pure MILP solvable by branch-and-bound/branch-and-cut.

**Assumptions stated:** uniform headway $h$; one blocked segment/track; fixed train directions; entry times fixed at origin; no station-track (platform) assignment conflicts; no rolling-stock/crew circulation constraints; disruption window fixed and known.

The generated model is largely sound, but I identified a few gaps: (1) the running-time coupling is only a lower bound — a train could idle on the segment, so an upper bound is needed to force consistency with the selected profile; (2) trains that do **not** reroute must be prevented from traversing the blocked track during the disruption window; (3) the delay definition should also capture earliness relative to the schedule when trains are held. Let me request a revision.

messages.content:
# Revised TRSMP MILP (Train Rescheduling with Rerouting and Disruption Window)

## 1. Sets and Indices

- $I = \{1,\dots,n\}$: trains, indexed $i$ (ordered by original timetable departure).
- $S = \{1,\dots,m\}$: track segments, indexed $s$; segment $s$ lies between stations $s$ and $s+1$; $b \in S$ is the **disrupted segment**.
- $P_{i,s}$: set of running-time profiles (routes/speed profiles) available to train $i$ on segment $s$. $P_{i,b}$ includes the normal route and alternative routes.
- $K_s$: set of physical tracks on segment $s$; each profile $p \in P_{i,s}$ uses exactly one track $k(p) \in K_s$ and a direction $\delta(p) \in \{+,-\}$.

## 2. Parameters

- $d^0_{i,s}, a^0_{i,s}$: scheduled departure/arrival times of train $i$ at the boundaries of segment $s$.
- $r_{i,s,p}$: running time of train $i$ on segment $s$ under profile $p$.
- $r^{\min}_{i,b}$: minimum running time of train $i$ on segment $b$ over all profiles (used in the blocking disjunction).
- $w_{i,s}$: minimum dwell time of train $i$ at station $s$.
- $h$: minimum headway (same for all segments; can be generalized to $h_{s,k}$).
- $M_t$: big-M for time constraints, $M_t \ge T^{max}$ (planning horizon length).
- $M_c$: big-M for cancellation relaxation, $M_c \ge T^{max}$.
- $T_0, T_1$: start and end of the disruption window on segment $b$ ($T_0 < T_1 \le T^{max}$).
- $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \theta \ge 0$: weights for total delay, arrival delay, rerouting cost, cancellation penalty.
- $\Delta^{\max}$: maximum allowed delay.

**Assumptions:** all times integer; $M_t, M_c \ge \max_i (a^0_{i,m} + \Delta^{\max})$; every profile $p$ has a well-defined track and direction; headway $h$ applies to trains in the same direction on the same track, and to opposite-direction trains on the same single-track segment (see constraint (H2)).

## 3. Variables

- $d_{i,s} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: departure time of train $i$ at the start of segment $s$.
- $a_{i,s} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$: arrival time of train $i$ at the end of segment $s$.
- $x_{i,s,p} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses profile $p$ on segment $s$.
- $y_{i,b} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ reroutes on segment $b$ (uses a non-default profile).
- $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ is cancelled.
- $z_i \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ (non-rerouted, non-cancelled) passes segment $b$ **before** $T_0$; 0 if it passes **after** $T_1$.
- $u_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$: 1 if train $i$ departs segment $s$ before train $j$ (ordering variable, defined for pairs sharing a track).

## 4. Objective

$$\min \; \alpha \sum_{i \in I} (a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m}) \;+\; \beta \sum_{i \in I} \max(0,\, a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m} - \Delta^{\max}) \;+\; \gamma \sum_{i \in I} y_{i,b} \;+\; \theta \sum_{i \in I} c_i$$

Linearized with auxiliary $\lambda_i \ge 0$:

$$\min \; \alpha \sum_i (a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m}) + \beta \sum_i \lambda_i + \gamma \sum_i y_{i,b} + \theta \sum_i c_i$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Profile selection** — exactly one profile per segment, unless cancelled:
$$\sum_{p \in P_{i,s}} x_{i,s,p} = 1 - c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

**(C2) Rerouting definition** (on segment $b$; $p^0$ = default profile):
$$y_{i,b} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,b} \setminus \{p^0\}} x_{i,b,p} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C3) Exact running-time coupling (tightened):**
$$a_{i,s+1} = d_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_{i,s}} r_{i,s,p}\, x_{i,s,p} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

(For cancelled trains the equality is relaxed by $M_c$; for non-cancelled trains the arrival **exactly equals** departure plus the selected profile's running time — no idling on the segment.)

**(C4) Dwell time:**
$$d_{i,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + w_{i,s+1} - M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S \setminus \{m\}$$

**(C5) Timetable lower bounds (no early departure/arrival):**
$$d_{i,s} \ge d^0_{i,s} - M_c\, c_i, \qquad a_{i,s} \ge a^0_{i,s} - M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I,\ \forall s \in S$$

**(C6) Maximum delay:**
$$a_{i,m} \le a^0_{i,m} + \Delta^{\max} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C7) Linearization of the max in the objective:**
$$\lambda_i \ge a_{i,m} - a^0_{i,m} - \Delta^{\max}, \qquad \lambda_i \ge 0 \qquad \forall i \in I$$

**(C8) Headway, same track, same direction.** For each segment $s$, track $k$, and each ordered pair $(i,j)$, $i \ne j$, both using profile(s) with track $k$ and same direction (enforce only when both non-cancelled):

Departure headway:
$$d_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - u_{i,j,s}) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$d_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - (1 - u_{i,j,s})) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

Arrival headway:
$$a_{j,s+1} \ge a_{i,s+1} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - u_{i,j,s}) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$a_{i,s+1} \ge a_{j,s+1} + h - M_t(3 - x^{k+}_{i,s} - x^{k+}_{j,s} - (1 - u_{i,j,s})) - M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

where $x^{k+}_{i,s} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,s}:\, k(p)=k,\, \delta(p)=+} x_{i,s,p}$ (analogously $x^{k-}$ for direction $-$; constraints are written for each direction).

**(H2) Headway on segment $b$, opposite directions on the same track.** For pairs $(i,j)$ whose chosen profiles on $b$ use the same track $k$ but opposite directions (this includes pairs where **both** reroute onto the same single track), the whole traversal must not overlap:

$$a_{j,b+1} \le d_{i,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - u_{i,j,b}) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$a_{i,b+1} \le d_{j,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - (1 - u_{i,j,b})) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

where $x^{k}_{i,b} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,b}: k(p)=k} x_{i,b,p}$ (any direction). **Explicitly: these arrival-headway constraints on segment $b$ apply to all pairs sharing a track there, including opposite-direction pairs when both reroute.**

**(C9) Disruption-window blocking.** For each train $i$ that does not reroute and is not cancelled, its traversal of segment $b$ must lie entirely before $T_0$ or entirely after $T_1$:

$$a_{i,b+1} \le T_0 + M_t(1 - z_i) + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$
$$d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1 - M_t\, z_i + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

Interpretation: if $y_{i,b}=0$ and $c_i=0$, then either $z_i=1$ forces $a_{i,b+1} \le T_0$ (clears the segment before the window opens), or $z_i=0$ forces $d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1$ (enters only after reopening; $r^{\min}$ guarantees the train cannot be inside the segment during $[T_0,T_1]$). If the train reroutes or is cancelled, both constraints are relaxed by $M_t y_{i,b}$ and $M_c c_i$ respectively.

**(C10) Variable domains:**
$$d_{i,s}, a_{i,s}, \lambda_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}; \quad x_{i,s,p}, y_{i,b}, c_i, z_i, u_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Explanation of Key Elements

- **(C3)** is the tightened coupling: the two-sided equality (lower bound from the original model plus the new upper bound merged into one equality) forces the traversal time to equal exactly the selected profile's running time; idling on a segment is impossible for non-cancelled trains.
- **(C9)** implements the disruption-window disjunction with a single binary $z_i$ per train; it is active only for non-rerouted, non-cancelled trains, so rerouting or cancellation provides the legal escape from the blockage.
- **(C8)/(H2)** use the ordering binaries $u_{i,j,s}$ with the standard 3-term big-M activation so headways are enforced only between trains actually sharing a track (and, on $b$, also across directions when both reroute onto the same track).
- **Big-M values:** $M_t \ge T^{max}$ (horizon), $M_c \ge T^{max}$; both must dominate any feasible time difference plus headway, e.g. $M_t = M_c = T^{max} + h$ is safe. All constraints are linear; integrality only on the declared binaries and integer times.

**(H2) Headway on segment $b$, opposite directions on the same track.** For pairs $(i,j)$ whose chosen profiles on $b$ use the same track $k$ but opposite directions (this includes pairs where **both** reroute onto the same single track), the whole traversal must not overlap:

$$a_{j,b+1} \le d_{i,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - u_{i,j,b}) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$
$$a_{i,b+1} \le d_{j,b} - h + M_t\,(3 - x^{k}_{i,b} - x^{k}_{j,b} - (1 - u_{i,j,b})) + M_c(c_i + c_j)$$

where $x^{k}_{i,b} = \sum_{p \in P_{i,b}: k(p)=k} x_{i,b,p}$ (any direction). **Explicitly: these arrival-headway constraints on segment $b$ apply to all pairs sharing a track there, including opposite-direction pairs when both reroute.**

**(C9) Disruption-window blocking.** For each train $i$ that does not reroute and is not cancelled, its traversal of segment $b$ must lie entirely before $T_0$ or entirely after $T_1$:

$$a_{i,b+1} \le T_0 + M_t(1 - z_i) + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$
$$d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1 - M_t\, z_i + M_t\, y_{i,b} + M_c\, c_i \qquad \forall i \in I$$

Interpretation: if $y_{i,b}=0$ and $c_i=0$, then either $z_i=1$ forces $a_{i,b+1} \le T_0$ (clears the segment before the window opens), or $z_i=0$ forces $d_{i,b} + r^{\min}_{i,b} \ge T_1$ (enters only after reopening; $r^{\min}$ guarantees the train cannot be inside the segment during $[T_0,T_1]$). If the train reroutes or is cancelled, both constraints are relaxed by $M_t y_{i,b}$ and $M_c c_i$ respectively.

**(C10) Variable domains:**
$$d_{i,s}, a_{i,s}, \lambda_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}; \quad x_{i,s,p}, y_{i,b}, c_i, z_i, u_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 6. Explanation of Key Elements

- **(C3)** is the tightened coupling: the two-sided equality (lower bound from the original model plus the new upper bound merged into one equality) forces the traversal time to equal exactly the selected profile's running time; idling on a segment is impossible for non-cancelled trains.
- **(C9)** implements the disruption-window disjunction with a single binary $z_i$ per train; it is active only for non-rerouted, non-cancelled trains, so rerouting or cancellation provides the legal escape from the blockage.
- **(C8)/(H2)** use the ordering binaries $u_{i,j,s}$ with the standard 3-term big-M activation so headways are enforced only between trains actually sharing a track (and, on $b$, also across directions when both reroute onto the same track).
- **Big-M values:** $M_t \ge T^{max}$ (horizon), $M_c \ge T^{max}$; both must dominate any feasible time difference plus headway, e.g. $M_t = M_c = T^{max} + h$ is safe. All constraints are linear; integrality only on the declared binaries and integer times.

The MILP should be described completely with equations and assumptions. The input is inspiration, so keep close to it, if you can and if information is missing, make reasonable assumptions and mark them as such. Do not ask questions. Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
